:::{#thm-lotus}
#### Law of the Unconscious Statistician (LOTUS)

**Discrete case.**
For any function $g$ of a *discrete* random variable $X$
[@wikipedia_law_of_the_unconscious_statistician]:

$$\E{g(X)} = \sum_{x \in \rangef{X}} g(x) \cd \P(X=x)$$

**Continuous case.**
For any function $g$ of a *continuous* random variable $X$ with density $\p(X=x)$:

$$\E{g(X)} = \int_{x \in \rangef{X}} g(x) \cd \p(X=x)\, dx$$

:::

::: proof

We prove the case of a [discrete random variable](random-variables.qmd#def-discrete-rv) first.
Let $Y = g(X)$.
For each $y \in \rangef{Y}$, the event $\{Y = y\}$ is the disjoint union
of the events $\{X = x\}$ over the values $x$ with $g(x) = y$,
and each $x \in \rangef{X}$ belongs to exactly one such group.

$$
\ba
\E{g(X)}
&= \E{Y} && \text{(substitution } Y = g(X) \text{)}
\\&= \sum_{y \in \rangef{Y}} y \cd \P(Y=y) && \text{(definition of expectation for discrete r.v.)}
\\&= \sum_{y \in \rangef{Y}} y \cd \sum_{\substack{x \in \rangef{X} \\ g(x) = y}} \P(X=x) && \text{(countable additivity over the disjoint events } \{X = x\} \text{)}
\\&= \sum_{y \in \rangef{Y}} \sum_{\substack{x \in \rangef{X} \\ g(x) = y}} y \cd \P(X=x) && \text{(distribute } y \text{ into the inner sum)}
\\&= \sum_{y \in \rangef{Y}} \sum_{\substack{x \in \rangef{X} \\ g(x) = y}} g(x) \cd \P(X=x) && \text{(} y = g(x) \text{ for every term of the inner sum)}
\\&= \sum_{x \in \rangef{X}} g(x) \cd \P(X=x) && \text{(the groups partition } \rangef{X} \text{)}
\ea
$$

The last step regroups a possibly infinite sum,
which is valid because $\E{g(X)}$ is defined only when the sum converges absolutely.

We prove the case of a [continuous random variable](random-variables.qmd#def-continuous-rv) $X$
and a [function](https://morrison-lab.github.io/mcs/functions.html#def-function) $g$ that is strictly increasing
and continuously [differentiable on](https://morrison-lab.github.io/mds/calculus-derivatives.html#def-differentiable) $\rangef{X}$,
with [inverse function](https://morrison-lab.github.io/mcs/functions.html#def-inverse-function) $h = \inv{g}$.
Let $Y = g(X)$.
Because $g$ is strictly increasing,
$\{Y \le y\} = \{X \le h(y)\}$,
so the [CDF](random-variables.qmd#def-cdf) of $Y$ is $\Pr(Y \le y) = \Pr(X \le h(y))$.
Differentiating with the chain rule gives the [density](random-variables.qmd#def-pdf) of $Y$:
$\p(Y=y) = \p(X=h(y)) \cd h'(y)$.

$$
\ba
\E{g(X)}
&= \E{Y} && \text{(substitution } Y = g(X) \text{)}
\\&= \int y \cd \p(Y=y)\,dy && \text{(definition of expectation for continuous r.v.)}
\\&= \int y \cd \p(X=h(y)) \cd h'(y)\,dy && \text{(density of } Y \text{)}
\\&= \int g(x) \cd \p(X=x)\,dx && \text{(substitute } y = g(x) \text{, so } h(y) = x \text{ and } h'(y)\,dy = dx \text{)}
\ea
$$

Each [integral](https://morrison-lab.github.io/mds/calculus-integration.html#def-riemann-integral) runs over the [range of](random-variables.qmd#def-range) its variable,
and $g$ carries $\rangef{X}$ onto $\rangef{Y}$.
For a strictly decreasing $g$, the same calculation holds
with $\Pr(Y \le y) = \Pr(X \ge h(y))$ and $\abs{h'(y)}$ in place of $h'(y)$.

:::
